response.text:
File Transfer Monitoring & Delivery Alerts — Files.com

# Know When The Right Files Didn’t Show Up

Tell Files.com what a correct delivery looks like — which files, in which folder, by when, in what shape — and it watches every window, opening an incident the moment data is missing, late, or malformed. Most file tools only tell you when a transfer fails. They can’t see the partner feed that silently never arrives. Files.com can, because it starts from what was supposed to happen and treats its absence as the failure.

## A Missing File Is The Failure Nobody Catches

In most file-transfer systems, “failure” means an error code — a transfer threw a 500, a connection dropped, a job errored. By that narrow definition a flow keeps reporting “succeeding” right up until a partner’s nightly file quietly stops coming. There was no transfer, so there was no error, so nothing alerted. Someone finds out days later when a downstream pipeline breaks and has to trace it back to a file that never arrived at 2 AM.

Files.com flips that around. A failure isn’t an error code. It’s the data you expected not showing up the way you expected it. This feature is called Expectations, and it lets you write down exactly what you expect: which files, from whom, by when, and what they should look like. Most file tools can only tell you a transfer technically completed. Files.com tells you whether the right thing actually happened.

## You Define What “Correct” Means

An Expectation captures a recurring delivery in four plain parts — the files to watch, the deadline, the shape they must take, and how much lateness you’ll accept.

### Which Files, And Where

Point an Expectation at a folder and a file pattern — your partner’s drop folder, only the *.csv files. That’s the set of files Files.com watches for.

### When They’re Due

Set the deadline — the 06:00 feed, the hourly package, the monthly close on the 3rd. Files.com reasons from that deadline, so a 06:00 cutoff records as 06:00 even if the check runs a minute later.

### What Shape They Take

Say what a correct delivery looks like: how many files, how big in total, which extensions, which named files must be present, what the file names must match, and which files must never appear.

### How Late Is Still Okay

Allow a grace window — accept the feed until 08:00 and mark it late rather than missing — and hold the window open a few extra minutes while a bursty multi-part upload is still arriving.

### Success — Data Is Ready

The right files arrived, on time, in the right shape. Files.com emits a durable “data is ready” signal that can kick off the next step — a downstream automation is now safe to run.

### Missing — Nothing Came

The deadline passed and nothing showed up. Files.com opens an incident and fires your failure alerts, so a vendor feed that silently stopped surfaces at 6 AM instead of when a downstream job breaks days later.

### Invalid — Something’s Wrong

Files arrived but didn’t meet your criteria — too few, the wrong extension, a required file absent, a forbidden temp file present. You learn exactly which rule failed, not just that “the transfer completed.”

### Late — Ready, But Past Deadline

The data arrived valid, but after the deadline you promised. Files.com can tell you the deadline was missed and, separately, that the data is now ready — two different facts your downstream teams both need.

## Evidence On Every Check, And A Trail You Can Prove

Every closed window keeps its evidence — the files that matched, the counts and bytes, and the exact criteria that passed or failed. An operator can see why a window passed or failed and which files were considered, instead of guessing. A missed deadline opens an incident you can acknowledge, snooze, comment on, and resolve, and it auto-resolves when a later window for the same feed comes through clean.

Together with the transfer engine’s integrity checks and the audit log, Expectations let you prove — not assume — that a critical file was delivered correctly and on time. That’s exactly the proof an auditor or a partner SLA asks for. See what each plan includes on the pricing page.

## How Teams Watch The Files They Are Owed

The same four checks show up wherever partners, custodians and agencies deliver on a schedule.

### The Custodian File Before The Trading Day

A check declares that the custodian’s positions file is due by six in the morning with at least one file over a minimum size, and the operations team hears about a miss while there is still time to call, not when the portfolio report is wrong.

### The Batch Counted Before It Is Pulled

A partner’s overnight batch is expected as forty files. The check confirms all forty, or names the missing sequence numbers, before the downstream job runs on a partial set. A short batch stops looking like a finished one.

### A Slack Or Teams Message When The Vendor Uploads

Arrival events post to the channel the team watches and can trigger the next workflow step, so the morning ritual of opening folders to eyeball counts ends.

### Regulatory Filings With Proof Of Arrival

The monthly submission to a state agency or an air district goes through a logged folder with a delivery check on it, so the filing team can show which cycle arrived, when, and who touched the file.

## File-Delivery Monitoring Questions

What teams ask about catching missing, late, and malformed file deliveries before a downstream process fails.

### What is file-delivery monitoring on Files.com?

Files.com file-delivery monitoring is a feature called Expectations: you define what a correct delivery looks like for a recurring file flow — which files, in which folder, by when, in what shape — and Files.com checks every window against that definition. When the data is missing, late, or malformed it opens an incident; when the delivery is correct it emits a data-ready signal.

### How is this different from a transfer alert?

A transfer alert tells you a transfer threw an error. Expectations tell you whether the right thing actually happened. A flow can report “succeeding” right up until a partner’s nightly file silently stops arriving — there was no transfer to fail. Expectations catch the absence of expected data, which a normal error alert never sees.

### What can I check about the files that arrive?

You can require a file count, a total size, allowed extensions, a filename pattern every file must match, and specific named files (each with its own size and count rules). You can also forbid files — say no *.tmp or *.partial may appear. The checks look at file metadata: names, sizes, counts, and extensions.

### Can it tell a partner what went wrong with their feed?

Yes, and precisely. Because Files.com knows exactly what you expected, it produces specific feedback — “your 06:00 feed was 40 minutes late and missing manifest.json” — instead of a vague “transfer failed.” That turns partner troubleshooting from a guessing game into a clear conversation.

### Does it inspect the contents inside the files?

Yes. Expectations check file metadata (names, sizes, counts, extensions, and which files are present or forbidden), and Expectations Content Validation reads inside the file: a Files TransformScript decides pass or fail against the parsed contents, with CSV, TSV, XLSX, XML, JSON, NDJSON, YAML, HL7, X12, and EDIFACT parsed automatically.

### Can a check trigger work automatically?

Yes. A failed window can trigger a failure automation or alert; a successful window emits a data-ready signal that can trigger downstream processing. Expectations watch and verify — they never move or change your files. They tell your automations and syncs when it’s safe to act.
